name: Salpingitis isthmica nodosa
aliases: diverticular disease of the fallopian tube

clinicalPearls: Characterised by nodular thickening of the isthmic portion of the fallopian tube, with diverticula of tubal epithelium extending into a hypertrophied muscular wall
Despite its name, it is a non-infective structural process rather than active infection of the tube
It is an important association of both subfertility and tubal ectopic pregnancy
The condition is frequently bilateral and may be identified when investigating infertility
Hysterosalpingography characteristically shows small diverticular outpouchings of contrast at the isthmus, giving a nodular appearance
Definitive confirmation is histological, demonstrating epithelial diverticula surrounded by hypertrophic smooth muscle
Because tubal function is compromised, in vitro fertilisation, which bypasses the tube, is often the most effective route to pregnancy
reference.pathophysiology: In salpingitis isthmica nodosa, the mucosal epithelium of the tubal isthmus forms diverticula that burrow into a surrounding, hypertrophied muscular layer, producing palpable and radiological nodularity. The cause is uncertain and may relate to previous chronic inflammation or to an adenomyosis-like ingrowth of epithelium into the muscularis. The distorted, partially obstructed tube impairs gamete and embryo transport, which underlies both the reduced fertility and the increased risk of tubal implantation of an embryo.
additionalDifferentials: Genital tract tuberculosis affecting the tube
additionalInvestigations: Hysterosalpingography demonstrating diverticular outpouchings and nodularity at the isthmus
Laparoscopy with chromopertubation to assess tubal patency and appearance
Histological examination, which provides the definitive diagnosis
Transvaginal ultrasound, which is of limited value but helps exclude other pelvic pathology
Assessment of overall fertility status, including partner and ovulatory factors
redFlags: Ectopic pregnancy in a woman known to have the condition
Significant subfertility requiring specialist reproductive input
Features suggesting coexisting tuberculous or other tubal disease
Acute pain that could indicate tubal implantation of a pregnancy
reference.prognosis: The lesion is benign, but it carries a meaningful impact on fertility and a raised risk of ectopic pregnancy; assisted conception that bypasses the tube generally offers the best chance of a successful pregnancy.
pitfalls: Failing to recognise the subtle diverticular changes on imaging
Not counselling the woman about the increased risk of ectopic pregnancy
Attempting reconstructive tubal surgery, which has limited success
Overlooking the diagnosis as a cause of otherwise unexplained subfertility
management: In vitro fertilisation that bypasses the diseased tube as the treatment offering the best chance of pregnancy
Salpingectomy of an affected, obstructed or hydrosalpinx-bearing tube before assisted conception to improve implantation
Microsurgical tubal resection and reanastomosis of the isthmic segment in carefully selected younger women desiring natural conception
Counselling on the raised risk of tubal ectopic pregnancy, with early ultrasound in any future pregnancy to confirm intrauterine location
Prompt treatment of an ectopic pregnancy with methotrexate or surgery as appropriate
Assessment and management of coexisting fertility factors, including ovulatory and male factors
Referral to reproductive medicine for individualised fertility planning
